channel.title: Acme: Science Fiction and Fantasy News
channel.description: Science fiction and fantasy fandom news, publishing, conventions, and history.

item.title: Jayant V. Narlikar’s Marathi cyber-thriller Virus reaches English readers
item.description: Arizona State University’s Center for Science and the Imagination published its announcement on September 1 for the November 17 release of Virus, Jayant V. Narlikar’s 1996 Marathi science-fiction novel. The late astrophysicist’s cyber-thriller imagines a hostile computer virus threatening national infrastructure, pairing scientific speculation with political intrigue. This annotated English edition, issued with MIT Press, makes the novel widely available in English after three decades and adds essays, an interview, contextual notes and a bonus story. The November 17 publication is the current news peg; the source page predates it. For readers interested in non-Anglophone genre history, scientific authorship and archival recovery, the edition offers both a rediscovered novel and documentation of its place in Indian science fiction.
item.source: ASU Center for Science and the Imagination

item.title: Novacon 55 remembers John Dowd while asking fandom to adapt and sustain
item.description: A convention report published November 20 looks back at Novacon 55, held November 6–8 at the Palace Hotel in Buxton under the theme “Adapt and Sustain.” Guest of honor Una McCormack joined programming on adaptation, environmental fiction and the future of fandom. The weekend also included a wake for John Dowd, whose extraordinary run stretched from Novacon 12 in 1982 through Novacon 54 in 2024. That memorial gives the report unusual value as a record of British fan continuity, while panels on adaptations and “wet dystopias” show the convention engaging present concerns. The November 20 report is the news peg; its detailed account preserves both institutional memory and the texture of a current regional convention.

item.title: Utah adds Sarah J. Maas fantasy novel to statewide school ban list
item.description: The Salt Lake Tribune reported November 18 that Utah added Sarah J. Maas’s Kingdom of Ash to its statewide school-removal list after a third district barred the book on November 17. The fantasy novel becomes the list’s 45th title, triggering removal from every public-school library under Utah law. The report says schools must dispose of banned copies rather than redistribute them, making the decision consequential beyond a single district. The November 17 action and November 18 report provide the current time peg. For genre readers, the case joins a bestselling fantasy author to an expanding censorship mechanism and raises practical questions about collection policy, local review and the destruction of books already purchased for students.

item.title: Amazing Stories marks its centennial with a new issue and a new publisher
item.description: Amazing Stories announced its Fall 2026 issue on November 18, giving the magazine’s centennial year a consequential coda after publisher Steve Davidson’s death on November 4. Kermit Woodall is now publisher and says the revived title will continue Davidson’s mission; the issue mixes fiction, essays, poetry and film commentary while memorializing him. The date peg is unusually strong: Hugo Gernsback’s first issue appeared March 10, 1926, so 2026 is the magazine’s 100th anniversary. For fandom historians, the release is not routine publicity but evidence that the oldest science-fiction magazine brand is attempting another editorial succession while maintaining its Amazing Selects book imprint and online presence.

item.title: Paradiso 17 wins the 2026 National Book Award for Fiction
item.description: The National Book Foundation announced the 2026 winners on November 18 at its 77th ceremony in New York. Hannah Lillith Assadi’s Paradiso 17 won Fiction; the judges praised its time-bending portrait of a Palestinian man born before the Nakba, placing a structurally speculative novel at the center of a major American literary award. Salman Rushdie also received the Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters, a career honor with obvious resonance for fantasy readers and for the history of censorship battles. The Foundation says publishers submitted 1,912 books across five categories. The immediate time peg is the November 18 ceremony and winners announcement, rather than the books’ earlier publication dates.

item.title: Wisconsin sisters prepare to open a science-fiction and fantasy bookstore
item.description: In Business Madison reported on November 11 that sisters Katie Rittenhouse and Elizabeth Arpin plan to open Soulbound Books in downtown Waunakee, Wisconsin, in December 2026. They are converting the historic former Fred’s Meat Market at 112 West Main Street into an independent shop specializing in science fiction and fantasy, filling a bookselling gap of roughly a dozen miles around the town. Before opening, the owners are building local ties through pop-up events with nearby businesses. The date peg is the newly announced December opening. For genre readers, the story is a concrete institutional gain: a physical SFF-focused bookstore arriving when many independent shops face narrow margins and declining foot traffic.

item.title: Philcon opens its 90th-anniversary weekend with fandom history on the program
item.description: Philcon begins its 90th-anniversary gathering on November 20, 2026, and runs through November 22 in Cherry Hill, New Jersey. Founded in 1936 by the Philadelphia Science Fiction Society, it bills itself as the world’s first and longest-running science-fiction conference, though wartime years interrupted the annual sequence. Charlie Jane Anders is principal speaker, Donato Giancola artist guest of honor and Sarah Pinsker musical guest; a 1632 MiniCon honors Eric Flint’s shared-world series. The schedule also includes a panel explicitly celebrating nine decades of conventions and a time-travel ball. Alex Shvartsman’s November 18 post supplies a participant’s program and provides the immediate news peg for an anniversary with unusually deep institutional-fandom resonance.

item.title: FANAC adds a fresh cache of rare fanzines and convention photographs
item.description: FANAC’s November 18, 2026, update adds another densely packed layer to its fan-history archive. New scans include 11 APA-L tables of contents from 1969-70, three 1957 FAPA one-shots, the 1950 SAPS one-shot Bar-Rag, Steve Stiles’ 1966 Star Wagon and Richard E. Geis’s index to Science Fiction Review numbers 28-43. The project also added 122 photographs, including material from Noreascon 3, Corflu gatherings and Geri Sullivan and Pat Virzi’s LAcon V guest-of-honor presentation. The source page is a current update log rather than a historical publication, and it dates this batch explicitly to November 18. For readers interested in amateur press associations and the preservation of fannish ephemera, it is a substantial archival release rather than routine housekeeping.

item.title: Alex Shvartsman turns 51 after a year that added a new novel and more translation work
item.description: November 19, 2026, is the 51st birthday of writer, editor and translator Alex Shvartsman, born November 19, 1975, in Odesa. His career joins several corners of modern fandom: more than 120 short stories, the Unidentified Funny Objects humor anthologies, Future Science Fiction Digest, translations from Russian and novels including 2026’s The Best of All Possible Planets. He won the 2014 WSFA Small Press Award for “Explaining Cthulhu to Grandma” and has repeatedly appeared on BSFA and Canopus Award ballots. The linked Black Gate birthday essay was published November 19, 2018, so its source date predates today’s anniversary peg; it examines “Staff Meeting, as Seen by the Spam Filter” and offers a useful snapshot of his earlier career.

item.title: Alan Dean Foster turns 80 after helping put Star Wars on the page
item.description: November 18, 2026, is the 80th birthday of Alan Dean Foster, born November 18, 1946. Before audiences had seen Star Wars, Foster turned its screenplay and production art into the 1976 novelization published under George Lucas’s name. His contract also produced Splinter of the Mind’s Eye, the 1978 adventure conceived so it could support a relatively inexpensive film sequel if necessary. Foster went on to write more than 100 books, including the Humanx Commonwealth and Spellsinger series and novelizations for Alien, Star Trek and other franchises. The linked anniversary essay was published today and draws on Foster’s Texas A&M archive biography and first-person accounts, making the date both a career milestone and a reminder of how paperback novelizations expanded screen fandom.

item.title: Heinlein’s “Misfit” television adaptation reaches its 75th anniversary
item.description: On November 18, 1951—75 years ago today—CBS aired “Misfit,” the fourth episode of its live science-fiction anthology Out There. Joseph Kramm adapted Robert A. Heinlein’s 1939 Astounding story about young men reshaping an asteroid’s orbit, part of a twelve-episode series that also drew on stories by John D. MacDonald, Theodore Sturgeon, Katherine MacLean and Frank Belknap Long. Almost none of the broadcasts are known to survive, leaving schedules, scripts and contemporary notices to document an unusually serious early attempt to put magazine science fiction on television. The linked Amazing Stories retrospective was published in November 2017; the original broadcast date supplies today’s verified 75th-anniversary peg.

item.title: Steve Davidson, publisher who revived Amazing Stories, dies at 67
item.description: Publisher and editor Steve Davidson died November 4, 2026, at 67; the linked obituary was published November 5. Davidson acquired Amazing Stories in 2012, restored the landmark title as a website, and returned it to print through a successful 2018 crowdfunding campaign. He also co-edited a sequence of Best of Amazing Stories reprint anthologies and worked to keep the magazine’s history available while opening it to contemporary writers and artists. His death during Amazing’s centennial year gives the loss particular resonance for fandom: Davidson’s stewardship connected Hugo Gernsback’s 1926 institution to its current online incarnation and helped the oldest science-fiction magazine begin a second century.

item.title: M. John Harrison becomes the Booker Prize’s first science-fiction-world winner
item.description: M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize on November 9 for The End of Everything, a dystopian satire published by Serpent’s Tail. At 81, Harrison is the prize’s oldest winner; Booker chief executive Gaby Wood also called him its first laureate to emerge from the established science-fiction world. The £50,000 award crowns a career that shaped British New Wave and later space opera while repeatedly resisting narrow genre labels. It is also Serpent’s Tail’s first Booker victory. The linked official release is dated November 2, before the ceremony, and records the result and judges’ reasoning; the November 9 announcement is the news peg that brings Harrison’s long relationship with both literary and genre institutions into focus.

item.title: Starlog returns to print as an annual on its 50th anniversary
item.description: Starlog returned to newsstands on November 13 with issue 375, ending a 17-year absence from print and marking 50 years since the magazine’s 1976 debut. The revived title will appear annually under editor-in-chief Annalee Newitz, with a new logo based on the original design and a cover by Gabriel Yeganyan. For fans who learned genre news from its interviews, convention reports and production photography, the format matters as much as the revival: this is a physical magazine, not merely a familiar trademark attached to a website. Space.com published the linked preview on November 8, five days before release, making the anniversary comeback a current publishing event with unusually strong fandom-memory appeal.

item.title: Jean-Louis Trudel remembered one year after his death in Vilnius
item.description: November 17 marks one year since Canadian author, editor and science-fiction historian Jean-Louis Trudel died in Vilnius on November 17, 2025, while serving as a writer in residence. He was 58. The Montreal-born scholar trained in physics, astronomy and the history of science, wrote roughly 30 books, and became a central chronicler of French-language Canadian speculative fiction. He also collaborated with Yves Meynard under the shared name Laurent McAllister, linking literary production with the institutional memory he preserved as critic and historian. CIRST published the linked memorial on November 20, 2025, three days after his death; today’s first anniversary supplies the verified time peg for revisiting a career that connected francophone fandom, publishing and scholarship.
item.source: Centre interuniversitaire de recherche sur la science et la technologie
